questions.q: What does the editorial say has replaced political rule as the basis of influence in the modern age?
options: Control of farmland
Not quite. The article says: Organisation and industrial infrastructure – peaceful economic strength.
Larger armies
Not quite. The article says: Organisation and industrial infrastructure – peaceful economic strength.
Royal marriages
Not quite. The article says: Organisation and industrial infrastructure – peaceful economic strength.
Organisation and industrial infrastructure – peaceful economic strength
Yes. Military occupation has become irrelevant.
questions.rationale: “With the advent of mechanical power, political rule became irrelevant. Now, organization and infrastructure replaced political power.”

questions.q: What test does the article suggest before spending money on something?
options: Ask whether it can be returned
Not quite. The article says: Stop and ask whether it meets a real need or only a desire.
Ask whether the price will rise
Not quite. The article says: Stop and ask whether it meets a real need or only a desire.
Ask whether one’s neighbours own it
Not quite. The article says: Stop and ask whether it meets a real need or only a desire.
Stop and ask whether it meets a real need or only a desire
Right. Spending on mere desire is wastefulness one must answer for.
questions.rationale: “Take time off to seriously think whether this is for something that you truly need or for something that you simply desire.”

questions.q: Looking at the vast universe, what two discoveries does the article say a person makes?
options: That the earth is ordinary, and that life is common
Not quite. The article says: That there is an all-powerful Creator and Sustainer, and that man is utterly helpless without Him.
That man is master of nature, and needs no help
Not quite. The article says: That there is an all-powerful Creator and Sustainer, and that man is utterly helpless without Him.
That there is an all-powerful Creator and Sustainer, and that man is utterly helpless without Him
Yes. Daily life teaches the same helplessness.
That the universe is empty, and has no order
Not quite. The article says: That there is an all-powerful Creator and Sustainer, and that man is utterly helpless without Him.
questions.rationale: “Firstly, the existence of an All-Powerful God, who is its Creator as well as its Sustainer… the second discovery will be that of the utter helplessness of man.”

questions.q: What does the article call a “psychological proof” of God’s existence?
options: The pleasure of success
Not quite. The article says: The feeling of dependence that every person meets in loss, sickness, age and death.
The comfort of belonging to a community
Not quite. The article says: The feeling of dependence that every person meets in loss, sickness, age and death.
The feeling of dependence that every person meets in loss, sickness, age and death
Well read. Our nature calls out that we need God.
The fear of being alone at night
Not quite. The article says: The feeling of dependence that every person meets in loss, sickness, age and death.
questions.rationale: “This feeling or realization is a psychological proof of God’s existence. Every person necessarily encounters this psychological experience.”

questions.article: Religion, a Divine Not a Social Phenomenon
questions.q: The article begins with nuclear energy, which can be misused for weapons. What point about religion does this lead to?
options: A thing should be judged on its own merit, not by its misuse – Islam by its texts, not by what some Muslims do
Correct. Theory must be separated from practice.
Religion changes with each society
Not quite. The article says: A thing should be judged on its own merit, not by its misuse – Islam by its texts, not by what some Muslims do.
Religion is as dangerous as nuclear energy
Not quite. The article says: A thing should be judged on its own merit, not by its misuse – Islam by its texts, not by what some Muslims do.
Science and religion should be kept apart
Not quite. The article says: A thing should be judged on its own merit, not by its misuse – Islam by its texts, not by what some Muslims do.
questions.rationale: “The harmfulness or benefits of a concept or phenomenon relates to its user… If one wishes to understand Islam, one must look at it apart from the Muslims.”

questions.q: According to the article, to whom is respect due?
options: To members of one’s own faith
Not quite. The article says: To every human being, of any religion or community, even where there are differences.
To elders and rulers only
Not quite. The article says: To every human being, of any religion or community, even where there are differences.
To every human being, of any religion or community, even where there are differences
Yes. It is man’s birthright.
To those who first show respect
Not quite. The article says: To every human being, of any religion or community, even where there are differences.
questions.rationale: “Everyone whether of one’s own religion or of any other religious tradition… is worthy of respect… human beings are to be respected despite their differences.”

questions.q: Where does the article say our love and devotion for God find expression in this world?
options: In how much we know
Not quite. The article says: In our relations with other human beings.
In our relations with other human beings
Right. This is where faith is tested.
In withdrawing from society
Not quite. The article says: In our relations with other human beings.
In the size of our places of worship
Not quite. The article says: In our relations with other human beings.
questions.rationale: “Our love and devotion for God finds expression in this world in the form of our relations with other human beings.”

questions.q: How does the article describe the relation between ritual and the inner spirit of religion?
options: Ritual is a later addition of no value
Not quite. The article says: Ritual is the outward expression of the spirit – like a shell to its kernel.
Ritual is opposed to the spirit
Not quite. The article says: Ritual is the outward expression of the spirit – like a shell to its kernel.
Ritual is the outward expression of the spirit – like a shell to its kernel
Yes. The kernel matters most, but the shell has its use.
Ritual is the whole of religion
Not quite. The article says: Ritual is the outward expression of the spirit – like a shell to its kernel.
questions.rationale: “Rituals are not just a set of rites; in fact, they are the external expression of the inner content of religion… like a nutshell without a kernel.”

questions.q: When a person performs a ritual while its spirit is, for the time, absent, what value does the article still see in it?
options: It impresses other people
Not quite. The article says: It serves as a regular reminder that keeps awareness of religion alive.
None whatever
Not quite. The article says: It serves as a regular reminder that keeps awareness of religion alive.
It serves as a regular reminder that keeps awareness of religion alive
Exactly. “A reminder of spirit through routine.”
It earns the same reward as with the spirit
Not quite. The article says: It serves as a regular reminder that keeps awareness of religion alive.
questions.rationale: “This minimum state is not totally worthless… It maintains the consciousness of religion and keeps one mindful of it.”

questions.q: Which four traits did the Prophet name as marks of hypocrisy?
options: Silence, shyness, caution and thrift
Not quite. The article says: Betraying a trust, speaking falsehood, breaking promises, and turning quarrelsome in a dispute.
Pride of birth, wealth, learning and beauty
Not quite. The article says: Betraying a trust, speaking falsehood, breaking promises, and turning quarrelsome in a dispute.
Betraying a trust, speaking falsehood, breaking promises, and turning quarrelsome in a dispute
Well read. To have even one is a flaw to be given up.
Poverty, illness, old age and ignorance
Not quite. The article says: Betraying a trust, speaking falsehood, breaking promises, and turning quarrelsome in a dispute.
questions.rationale: “He betrays the trust of others; he speaks falsehood; he does not keep his promises; and when differences arise, he will not hesitate to fight.”
